summary: Defines a metric for one-way packet loss across Internet paths. It was replaced by RFC 7680.

eli5.summary: A precise way to count how many messages never arrive on a one-way trip.

questions: how is packet loss measured in ippm
why use poisson sampling for network measurement
what counts as a lost packet
subtitle: A precise definition of what it means for a packet to be lost on a one-way Internet path, and how to sample and average it.

tldr.problem: Packet loss affects real-time applications and the throughput of transport protocols, but different measurement tools could report incomparable numbers unless the quantity is defined exactly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a single-packet metric, Type-P-One-way-Packet-Loss (0 if the packet arrived, 1 if it did not), a sample of such values taken at Poisson-distributed times, and an average of the sample.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2680 was a Proposed Standard but has been obsoleted by RFC 7680, which is the current definition.

today: RFC 2680 has been obsoleted by RFC 7680, which is the current definition of the one-way packet loss metric. It was a Proposed Standard.

sections.title: Why Measure One-way Loss
sections.content:
RFC 2680 defines a metric for one-way packet loss across Internet paths. It builds on the IPPM Framework (RFC 2330) and is parallel in structure to the one-way delay metric (RFC 2679). The RFC uses the key words of RFC 2119 not for protocol behavior but to make results from two implementations comparable and to flag cases where an implementation could perturb the network.

Loss matters because some applications perform badly, or not at all, when end-to-end loss is large, because excessive loss makes real-time applications hard to support, and because higher loss makes it harder for transport protocols to sustain high bandwidths.

It measures one direction instead of round trip because the forward and reverse paths may differ (asymmetric paths), may have different queueing, may be provisioned differently in quality-of-service networks, and because an application such as a TCP file transfer may depend mostly on the data direction. The RFC leaves it outside its scope to say how loss metrics apply to specific problems.
sections.eli5: Looking at only one direction tells you exactly where trouble is. A round trip mixes two different roads together, so you cannot tell which one is bad.

sections.title: The Singleton Loss Metric
sections.content:
The basic building block is the singleton Type-P-One-way-Packet-Loss, with parameters Src and Dst (IP addresses of hosts) and T (a time). Its value is 0 if Src sent the first bit of a Type-P packet to Dst at wire-time T and Dst received it, and 1 if Dst did not receive it. Equivalently, loss is 0 exactly when the one-way delay is a finite value and 1 when delay is undefined.

The RFC settles several edge cases. A packet that arrives corrupted counts as lost. A packet duplicated along the way so that several non-corrupt copies arrive counts as received. A fragmented packet that is never reassembled counts as lost. A method must also distinguish loss from a very large but finite delay; the RFC mentions the 255 seconds theoretical upper bound on IP packet lifetimes as one simple option.

The RFC also defines time terms: synchronization, accuracy, resolution and skew, as used in the Framework. Times are measured in seconds relative to UTC.
sections.eli5: For each packet, write 0 if it got there and 1 if it did not. A packet that arrives all scrambled counts as not arriving, and a packet that arrives twice still counts as arriving.

sections.title: Methodology and Poisson Sampling
sections.content:
One possible method has Src and Dst keep their clocks synchronized, builds a Type-P test packet, places a timestamp in it, and sends it. If it arrives within a reasonable period of time, loss is 0; otherwise it is 1. The threshold for reasonable is a parameter of the method. Packet format, how Dst knows when to expect the packet, and how clocks are synchronized are outside the scope of the RFC.

To get a statistical picture, the RFC defines Type-P-One-way-Packet-Loss-Poisson-Stream. Given a start time T0, an end time Tf and an average rate lambda, a pseudo-random Poisson process picks the sending times between T0 and Tf, and the singleton is measured at each time. The sample is the sequence of (time, loss) pairs. The interval between successive times averages 1/lambda.

Poisson sampling is chosen to avoid self-synchronization effects and to be statistically as unbiased as possible. The RFC does not constrain lambda except to warn that too high a rate perturbs the network and causes congestion, while too low a rate may miss interesting behavior. Implementations must handle out-of-order arrival of test packets, and good pseudo-random number generators are needed. The Framework describes using the Anderson-Darling test to check the Poisson process.

The RFC notes that loss rates seen by transport connections such as TCP are not unbiased samples: TCP sends in bursts that can induce loss and adapts its rate to reduce the loss it sees.
sections.eli5: Instead of sending test packets on a steady beat, which could line up with other traffic, you send them at random moments that average out to a chosen pace, so the count is fair.

sections.title: The Average and Sources of Error
sections.content:
The one statistic defined is Type-P-One-way-Packet-Loss-Average: the average of all the L values in the sample, undefined if the sample is empty. The RFC's example sample of five singletons with a single loss gives an average of 0.2.

The RFC says healthy Internet paths should operate at loss rates below 1%, so telling apart fractions of 1% over one-minute periods might need several hundred samples per minute, which means a larger lambda than one would ordinarily want.

There are three sources of error: clock synchronization between Src and Dst, the loss threshold (which is related to synchronization), and resource limits in the receiving instrument. A too-low threshold or poorly synchronized clocks can make a packet with finite delay look lost, and a receiving instrument that drops a packet makes the network look worse than it is. Instruments should be calibrated so that arriving packets are rarely counted as lost. The loss measurement is less sensitive to clock synchronization than delay is.
sections.eli5: If one packet in five goes missing, the average is 0.2. Your counting tools can make mistakes too, like a stopwatch that is a bit off, so you must check they are accurate.

sections.title: Reporting and Security
sections.content:
Results MUST be reported with their context: the exact Type-P of the test packets, the loss threshold (or the method used to tell large delay from loss), the degree of clock synchronization and calibration results, and, if possible, the path traversed. The RFC says exact path knowledge is generally impractical, since options such as record route are rarely supported and would worsen the observed performance.

The security section names two concerns. Measurements are active and inject packets, so their parameters MUST be chosen to add only trivial traffic; too much can skew results and in extreme cases cause congestion and denial of service. The measurements can also be harmed if routers give measurement traffic different priority, or if an attacker injects artificial traffic that is accepted as legitimate, which would artificially lower the loss rate. Methods SHOULD make measurement traffic hard to distinguish from normal traffic, and digital signatures may be used against injection. Privacy concerns are limited because, unlike passive measurement, there is no release of existing user data.
sections.eli5: Always write down how you ran your test so others can trust the result. And do not send so many test packets that you clog the road you are measuring.

items.label: Received
items.desc: Dst received the Type-P packet that Src sent at wire-time T.

items.label: Lost
items.desc: Dst did not receive it; a corrupted packet and an unreassembled fragment also count as lost.
